q: A 'basic budget' in budgetary control is best described as:

options.A: A budget prepared for a single month only, in an emergency
options.B: A budget established for a long period, expressing the basic conditions and standards of a base position, which serves as a yardstick with reference to which the current budgets for successive periods are prepared after adjusting for current conditions
options.C: Another name for the cash budget of an enterprise
options.D: A budget which contains only the fixed costs of an enterprise

q: The 'practical capacity' of a plant, for the purpose of preparing its budgets, means:

options.A: The maximum capacity that remains after deducting the capacity unavoidably lost through weekly holidays, normal repairs and maintenance, setting-up time and other normal interruptions from the theoretical maximum capacity
options.B: The theoretical maximum output obtainable if the plant worked continuously without any stoppage of any kind
options.C: The output actually achieved by the plant in the previous year
options.D: The output which the sales department expects to sell during the budget period

q: Under the objective-and-task method of preparing an advertising budget, the amount to be spent on advertising is arrived at by:

options.A: Taking a fixed percentage of the sales of the previous year
options.B: Spending exactly the same amount as the principal competitor is spending
options.C: Taking whatever funds remain after all other budgets have been provided for
options.D: Defining the advertising objectives to be achieved, determining the specific tasks needed to achieve them and estimating the cost of performing those tasks, the total of such costs being the advertising budget

q: The repairs and maintenance budget of a factory is prepared primarily on the basis of:

options.A: A fixed percentage of the sales value of the products manufactured
options.B: The depreciation charged on the plant and machinery during the period
options.C: The planned maintenance programme of the enterprise, that is, the preventive maintenance schedules, the planned overhauls and the expected breakdown repairs judged from the age, condition and past repair history of each machine
options.D: The amount spent on maintenance in the previous year, increased by a uniform percentage in every case

q: Under the sales-force composite method of forecasting sales for the sales budget, the sales forecast is built up by:

options.A: Applying a statistical trend line to the sales of the past ten years, without consulting anyone
options.B: Obtaining from each salesman an estimate of the sales expected in his own territory, and reviewing, adjusting and aggregating these estimates at the area and head-office levels
options.C: Asking the production manager to state the quantity the factory can produce
options.D: Adopting the sales target fixed by the trade association for the whole industry

q: A factory must deliver 45,000 good units during the budget period. Experience shows that 10% of the units put into production are spoiled beyond rectification and yield no good output. The number of units that must be put into production is:

options.A: 49,500 units
options.B: 45,000 units
options.C: 50,000 units
options.D: 40,500 units

q: Once the master budget of an enterprise has been approved, its effect on the authority of the departmental managers is that:

options.A: It authorises each manager to incur expenditure within the limits and for the purposes provided in his budget, while expenditure in excess of a budget head requires prior approval even if a saving exists under some other head
options.B: It authorises each manager to spend any amount he likes, provided the total expenditure of the enterprise remains within the master budget
options.C: It takes away all authority of the managers to incur any expenditure during the year
options.D: It authorises the managers to transfer savings from one budget head to another at their own discretion, without informing anyone

q: Budgets exercise a 'feedforward' type of control in an enterprise because:

options.A: They are prepared only after the actual results of a period are known
options.B: They merely record the variances that have already occurred in past periods
options.C: They are used only for punishing the managers responsible for past failures
options.D: By projecting the results of the planned operations in advance, they reveal likely future problems, such as a cash shortage or a capacity bottleneck in a coming period, in time for corrective action to be taken before the problem actually arises

q: A departmental manager, in order to show a favourable cost variance for his department for the current year, postpones essential maintenance of his machines and cancels the training programme of his staff, although both will harm the enterprise in the following years. This behaviour is an example of:

options.A: Zero-based budgeting
options.B: Sub-optimisation, in which a manager pursues the goal of his own budget centre at the expense of the objectives of the enterprise as a whole
options.C: Management by exception
options.D: Flexing of the budget for the actual level of activity

q: A production programme requires 18,000 productive labour hours. The normal working hours available are 16,000, paid at the basic rate of Rs 60 per hour, and the balance of the hours will be worked as overtime, for which a premium of 50% of the basic rate is payable in addition to the basic rate. The direct labour cost to be provided in the budget is:

The product of an enterprise is in heavy demand only during a few months of the year and is little demanded in the remaining months. In preparing its annual sales and production budgets, the correct treatment of this seasonal pattern is that:

options.A: The annual budget should be phased month by month in proportion to the demand expected in each month, instead of being divided equally into twelve parts, so that production, stocks and cash are planned according to the seasonal pattern
options.B: The annual budget should always be divided into twelve equal monthly parts, whatever the pattern of demand
options.C: No monthly budgets should be prepared at all for a seasonal product
options.D: The budget should provide for the peak month's demand in every month of the year

q: In preparing the materials purchase budget in terms of value, the quantity of material to be purchased should be valued at:

options.A: The prices ruling on the date on which the budget is prepared, in every case
options.B: The prices at which the material was purchased in the previous year
options.C: The prices expected to prevail at the time when the purchases will actually be made during the budget period, as forecast at the time of budgeting
options.D: The selling price of the finished product in which the material will be used

q: An enterprise wishes to provide in its budget for expenditure of an unforeseen nature that may arise during the year. The sound way of making this provision is to:

options.A: Deliberately overstate every item of departmental expenditure by a small percentage, without disclosing it
options.B: Show a separate, clearly identified contingency allowance in the budget, to be drawn upon only for genuinely unforeseen items with proper approval
options.C: Make no mention of unforeseen expenditure anywhere and meet it by exceeding the budget heads
options.D: Reduce the budgeted sales by an arbitrary amount and treat the difference as the contingency provision

q: For the various functional budgets of an enterprise to be capable of being coordinated and consolidated into a master budget, it is essential that:

options.A: Each department should prepare its budget on whatever assumptions it considers best for itself
options.B: The budgets should be prepared in different currencies by different departments
options.C: The sales budget should use one set of selling prices and the production budget a different set
options.D: All the functional budgets are built on a common set of assumptions regarding matters such as the level of prices, wage rates, the sales mix and the accounting policies to be followed

q: An enterprise purchases stock of Rs 3,00,000 entirely on credit from its suppliers, the stock remaining unsold at the end of the period. The effect of this transaction on its working capital is that:

options.A: Both gross working capital and net working capital increase by Rs 3,00,000
options.B: Net working capital increases by Rs 3,00,000 and gross working capital remains unchanged
options.C: Gross working capital increases by Rs 3,00,000, while net working capital remains unchanged, because current liabilities increase by the same amount as the current assets
options.D: Neither gross nor net working capital is affected in any way

q: The total annual cash operating outlay of an enterprise is Rs 73,00,000 and the length of its cash conversion cycle is 73 days, reckoning a year of 365 days. On the cash turnover method, the minimum operating cash balance it needs to maintain is:

An enterprise uses a raw material, such as an agricultural produce, which is available in plenty and at low prices only during a short harvest season of the year. Its working capital requirement will be comparatively heavy mainly because:

options.A: It must buy and stock, during the short season, a large part of its whole year's requirement of the material, so that a large amount of funds remains blocked in raw material stock for a long period
options.B: Its customers pay it more promptly during the harvest season
options.C: Its bankers refuse to finance any seasonal industry
options.D: The material purchased in the season is not recorded in its books at all

q: The dividend policy of an enterprise has a bearing on its working capital position because:

options.A: Dividends can be paid only out of the cash credit limit sanctioned by the bank
options.B: The payment of dividends increases the stock of finished goods of the enterprise
options.C: Dividends have no connection of any kind with the finances of an enterprise
options.D: A liberal policy of paying out a large part of the profits as dividend leaves less profit to be retained and ploughed back for financing working capital, and so increases the dependence of the enterprise on outside sources of finance

q: An enterprise which enjoys a high credit standing and a reputation for prompt payment will generally require less of its own working capital mainly because:

options.A: It is exempt from maintaining any stock of materials
options.B: Its products are sold at higher prices than those of its competitors
options.C: Suppliers are willing to grant it longer credit and bankers are readier to finance it, so that a larger part of its current assets is financed by others and its own funds are blocked for a shorter period
options.D: It is not required to pay wages to its workers in cash

q: A very rigorous collection policy, under which customers are pressed hard and legal steps are threatened on the slightest delay in payment, may prove counter-productive for an enterprise because:

options.A: It will always increase the bad debts of the enterprise
options.B: While it may reduce bad debts and the investment in receivables, the ill-will it creates may drive customers to competitors and reduce the sales and profits of the enterprise by more than the saving achieved
options.C: It has no effect at all on the customers of the enterprise
options.D: It is prohibited by the law relating to contracts in all circumstances

q: 'Packing credit' provided by a bank to an exporter is:

options.A: A pre-shipment advance granted to enable the exporter to purchase, process and pack the goods meant for export, which is normally liquidated out of the export proceeds or out of post-shipment finance
options.B: A loan granted to a customer for packing his household goods before shifting his residence
options.C: A post-shipment advance granted against shipping documents after the goods have been exported
options.D: An advance granted to an importer for paying the customs duty on imported goods

q: In contracting and construction enterprises, 'retention money' increases the working capital requirement of the contractor because:

options.A: The contractor is required to deposit the retention money with the Government in cash
options.B: Retention money is an additional tax levied on contractors by the client
options.C: The contractor has to pay retention money to his own workers every month
options.D: The client retains a percentage of every running bill and releases it only after the work is completed and the defect-liability period is over, so that a part of the contractor's dues remains blocked as a receivable for a long period

q: The annual cost of production of an enterprise is Rs 54,75,000 and its finished goods remain in stock, on an average, for 20 days before being sold, reckoning a year of 365 days. The amount of working capital blocked in the stock of finished goods is:
Under the practice of 'seasonal dating' in the sale of seasonal goods, an enterprise offers credit terms under which:

options.A: The goods are invoiced at a lower price during the season than in the off-season
options.B: Goods are shipped to buyers during the off-season, but the dating of the invoice, and hence the start of the credit period and the due date for payment, is postponed to a date near the beginning of the selling season, so that the buyers can stock the goods early without having to pay for them until the season starts
options.C: The customers are required to pay for the goods before the goods are despatched to them
options.D: No credit at all is allowed on the sale of seasonal goods

q: A bank overdraft, as a means of financing the working capital of an enterprise, is a facility under which:

options.A: The customer is allowed to draw on his current account in excess of the credit balance standing in it, up to a sanctioned limit, the facility being repayable on demand and generally meant for temporary requirements
options.B: The bank purchases the bills of exchange drawn by the customer on his buyers
options.C: The bank opens a letter of credit in favour of the supplier of the customer
options.D: The customer deposits a fixed sum with the bank for a fixed period at a fixed rate of interest

q: A bank levies a 'commitment charge' on the working capital limits sanctioned by it. This charge is levied:

options.A: On the amount of the limit actually utilised by the borrower throughout the year
options.B: As a penalty for a default in the repayment of a term loan
options.C: Only on the non-fund-based limits, such as guarantees, sanctioned to the borrower
options.D: On the unutilised portion of the sanctioned limit, in order to compensate the bank for keeping funds committed for the borrower and to discourage borrowers from asking for limits far in excess of their genuine requirements

q: Where a bank finances the working capital of an enterprise against the assignment of its book debts, the arrangement is that:

options.A: The book debts are sold outright to the bank and can never be recovered by the enterprise
options.B: The debtors of the enterprise become the shareholders of the bank
options.C: The book debts are assigned to the bank as security for the advance, so that the bank acquires the right to recover the dues from the debtors of the enterprise, particularly on the borrower's default, the debts remaining the property of the borrower subject to this charge
options.D: The bank itself takes over the entire sales organisation of the enterprise

q: An enterprise appoints consignees in distant markets and sends them large stocks of its goods for sale. From the standpoint of its working capital, the significant feature of this consignment stock is that:

options.A: The stock ceases to be an asset of the enterprise as soon as it is despatched to the consignees
options.B: The ownership of the goods remains with the enterprise until they are sold by the consignees, so its funds remain blocked in stock lying at distant places, often for long periods, in addition to the credit allowed after the sale
options.C: The consignees finance the entire working capital of the enterprise
options.D: Consignment stock is not included in the current assets of the enterprise

q: An enterprise which markets its products through a large number of its own depots and branch warehouses spread all over the country will generally require more working capital than a similar enterprise selling from a single central stock, mainly because:

options.A: Branch warehouses are exempt from the payment of rent and insurance
options.B: Customers of branch warehouses always pay in advance
options.C: The selling price at the branches is fixed by the Government
options.D: Stock has to be maintained at every stocking point, with its own minimum and safety levels at each, so that the aggregate stock carried in the pipeline is much larger than in a centralised system

q: In preparing a fund flow statement, the provision for taxation is treated as a non-current liability. The provision for taxation account shows: opening balance Rs 80,000; provision made during the year by transfer from the profit and loss account Rs 1,50,000; closing balance Rs 90,000. The income-tax actually paid during the year is:

The plant and machinery account (at written down value) of an enterprise shows an opening balance of Rs 5,00,000 and a closing balance of Rs 6,20,000. Depreciation charged during the year is Rs 60,000 and a machine having a book value of Rs 40,000 was sold during the year. The plant and machinery purchased during the year, which will be shown as an application of funds, is:

An enterprise has made a net loss of Rs 30,000 during a year, after charging depreciation of Rs 20,000 and preliminary expenses written off of Rs 5,000, and after crediting a profit of Rs 10,000 on the sale of its investments. The result of its operations, for the purpose of the fund flow statement, is:

options.A: Funds from operations of Rs 15,000
options.B: Funds lost in operations of Rs 15,000, which will be shown on the applications side of the fund flow statement
options.C: Funds lost in operations of Rs 5,000
options.D: Funds from operations of Rs 5,000

q: The debentures account of an enterprise shows an opening balance of Rs 4,00,000 and a closing balance of Rs 5,50,000. During the year, debentures of Rs 50,000 were redeemed. The fresh debentures issued during the year, to be shown as a source of funds, amount to:

In the cash flow statement of an enterprise prepared under AS-3, the income-tax paid by it during the year, where the tax is not specifically identifiable with any investing or financing transaction, is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities, since cash flows from taxes on income are ordinarily treated as operating unless they can be specifically identified with a financing or investing activity
options.B: Financing activities, in every case
options.C: Investing activities, in every case
options.D: No activity at all, tax paid being excluded from the cash flow statement

q: The operating expenses charged in the profit and loss account of an enterprise (excluding depreciation) are Rs 2,40,000. The outstanding expenses were Rs 30,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 45,000 at the end of the year, and the prepaid expenses were Rs 12,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 20,000 at the end of the year. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash paid in respect of these operating expenses is:
In a cash flow statement prepared by the indirect method, a fixed asset having a book value of Rs 70,000 is sold for Rs 88,000. The correct treatment of this transaction is that:

options.A: Only the profit of Rs 18,000 is shown as a cash inflow from investing activities
options.B: The profit of Rs 18,000, being included in the net profit, is deducted in arriving at the operating profit before working capital changes, and the full sale proceeds of Rs 88,000 are shown as a cash inflow from investing activities
options.C: The full sale proceeds of Rs 88,000 are added to the net profit in computing the cash from operating activities
options.D: Neither the profit nor the sale proceeds appear anywhere in the cash flow statement

q: An enterprise acquires machinery under a hire-purchase arrangement. During the year it pays only the initial deposit and two instalments in cash, the balance of the price remaining payable in future instalments. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, the correct treatment is that:

options.A: The full price of the machinery is shown as a cash outflow from investing activities in the year of acquisition
options.B: No amount at all is shown, because the machinery has been acquired on hire-purchase
options.C: The full price of the machinery is shown as a cash outflow from operating activities
options.D: Only the amount actually paid in cash during the year is shown as a cash flow, the unpaid portion being a non-cash investing and financing transaction which is excluded from the cash flow statement and disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements

q: A cash flow statement differs from a cash budget mainly in that:

options.A: The cash flow statement relates to the cash flows that have actually taken place during a past period, analysing them into operating, investing and financing activities, whereas the cash budget is a forecast of the cash receipts and payments expected in a future period
options.B: The cash budget relates to a past period and the cash flow statement to a future period
options.C: The cash flow statement is prepared only by Government departments
options.D: There is no difference at all between the two statements

q: During a year, an enterprise issues shares for cash for Rs 6,00,000, raises long-term borrowings of Rs 3,00,000, repays long-term borrowings of Rs 1,50,000 and pays dividends of Rs 2,50,000. Its net cash flow from financing activities is:

options.A: Rs 9,00,000 inflow
options.B: Rs 5,00,000 inflow
options.C: Rs 11,50,000 inflow
options.D: Rs 3,50,000 inflow

q: Under AS-3, the cash flows relating to interest and dividends received and paid, and the cash flows arising from taxes on income, are required to be:

options.A: Netted off against each other and shown as a single figure
options.B: Omitted from the cash flow statement altogether
options.C: Disclosed separately in the cash flow statement, so that the users can see the amounts involved under each of these heads
options.D: Shown only in the balance sheet of the enterprise and nowhere else

q: An enterprise repays a long-term loan by annual instalments, each instalment comprising a part of the principal and interest for the year, the interest having been charged in the profit and loss account. In the fund flow statement, the application of funds in respect of these instalments is:

options.A: The whole amount of the instalments paid, including the interest element
options.B: Only the principal element of the instalments, since the interest is a revenue charge already reflected in the profit and loss account and does not reduce the long-term liability
options.C: Nil, because the repayment of a loan is not an application of funds
options.D: Only the interest element of the instalments

q: As regards the method of presenting the cash flow from operating activities, Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3):

options.A: Prohibits the use of the direct method in all cases
options.B: Requires every enterprise to use the indirect method only
options.C: Has nothing to say about the choice between the direct and the indirect methods
options.D: Encourages the use of the direct method, because it provides information about the major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments which is not otherwise readily available, though the indirect method is also permitted

q: Under AS-3, an enterprise is required, in connection with its cash flow statement, to disclose:

options.A: The names of all the customers from whom cash was received during the year
options.B: The components of cash and cash equivalents, together with a reconciliation of the amounts reported in the cash flow statement with the equivalent items reported in the balance sheet
options.C: The cash balance expected to be held at the end of the next financial year
options.D: The details of every cash payment, however small, made during the year

q: In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method under AS-3, the cash received by a non-financial enterprise from royalties, fees and commissions for services rendered by it is shown as:

options.A: A cash inflow from financing activities
options.B: A cash inflow from investing activities
options.C: A cash receipt from operating activities, royalties, fees and commissions being among the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise
options.D: It is not shown in the cash flow statement at all

q: Under AS-3, 'financing activities' in a cash flow statement are the activities that:

options.A: Relate to the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets of the enterprise
options.B: Are the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise
options.C: Relate only to the cash kept in the cash box of the enterprise
options.D: Result in changes in the size and composition of the owners' capital and the borrowings of the enterprise

q: Loose tools (small tools) used in a factory are usually accounted for in cost accounts by:

options.A: Charging their full cost as a direct expense to the first job on which they are used
options.B: Revaluing them at the end of the period and charging the fall in value (depreciation) to factory overheads
options.C: Capitalising them permanently like plant and machinery, without providing for any depreciation
options.D: Ignoring them altogether, as the value of each tool is small

q: A mine pays royalty of Rs 10 per tonne of coal raised, subject to a minimum rent of Rs 1,00,000 per year. The output during the year is 8,000 tonnes. The amount actually payable to the landlord for the year is:
In the primary distribution of factory overheads, the storekeeping (stores department) expenses are most appropriately apportioned to the departments on the basis of:

options.A: The number of material requisitions raised by each department
options.B: The floor area occupied by each department
options.C: The direct wages paid in each department
options.D: The value of plant installed in each department

q: A job spends 60 machine hours in Department X, where overheads are absorbed at Rs 45 per machine hour, and 80 labour hours in Department Y, where overheads are absorbed at Rs 25 per labour hour. The total overhead charged to the job is:
Method study, as a technique of work study, is concerned with:

options.A: Determining the standard time for a job by stop-watch observation of the worker
options.B: Rating the relative worth of the different jobs in the factory
options.C: Assessing the merits and personal qualities of individual workers
options.D: The systematic recording and critical examination of existing methods of doing work, in order to develop an easier and more effective method

q: A contract for Rs 1,00,00,000 contains an escalation clause covering a rise in material prices. Materials account for 40% of the contract value. Material prices have risen by 10% over the base level. The escalation amount payable under the clause is:
Product life-cycle costing, as a costing approach, tracks and accumulates the costs of a product over:

options.A: The manufacturing stage of the product only
options.B: The whole life of the product, from its design and development through manufacture, marketing and after-sales service to its withdrawal
options.C: One accounting year at a time, like ordinary historical costing
options.D: The period for which the product remains in the finished goods store

q: A product sells at Rs 100 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 60 per unit and fixed costs of Rs 2,00,000. At present 10,000 units are sold. It is proposed to raise the price by 10%, which is expected to reduce the volume of sales by 15%. The profit under the proposal will be:
A job card maintained for a worker in a factory is primarily used to record:

options.A: The time at which the worker enters and leaves the factory gate
options.B: The leave applied for and availed of by the worker
options.C: The disciplinary action taken against the worker
options.D: The time spent by the worker on each job or operation, so that labour cost can be charged to jobs

q: The sales of a firm at full installed capacity are Rs 20,00,000. Its fixed costs are Rs 3,00,000 and the P/V ratio is 40%. The break-even point, expressed as a percentage of the full capacity sales, is:
A uniform costing manual, adopted by the member units of an industry which follows uniform costing, principally lays down:

options.A: The selling prices to be charged by each member unit for its products
options.B: The wages payable to the workers employed in each member unit
options.C: The common principles, methods and procedures of cost accounting — classification of costs, cost units, codes and forms — to be followed by all the member units
options.D: The production targets to be achieved by each member unit

q: A factory canteen incurs total costs of Rs 4,80,000 during a period and recovers Rs 1,20,000 from the employees who use it. The number of meals served during the period is 90,000. The net cost per meal borne by the factory is:
In railway traffic costing, terminal costs are those costs which are incurred at the originating and destination terminals — such as loading, unloading, booking and delivery — and which:

options.A: Increase in direct proportion to the distance the traffic is carried
options.B: Are recovered only from passengers and not from goods traffic
options.C: Form part of the line-haul cost of the movement
options.D: Do not vary with the distance over which the traffic is carried

q: A cinema hall has 400 seats and runs 3 shows a day for 30 days in a month. The average occupancy is 75% of the seats. The total operating cost for the month is Rs 8,10,000. The operating cost per man-show is:
'Job evaluation' in wage administration is the systematic process of:

options.A: Determining the relative worth of jobs in an organisation, so that a rational wage structure can be built
options.B: Assessing the merits and personal qualities of the worker holding a job
options.C: Measuring the time taken by a worker to complete a job
options.D: Fixing the piece rate for each job produced in the factory

q: In a process, 2,500 kg of material costing Rs 1,80,000 is introduced. Labour and overhead costs of the process are Rs 90,000. Normal loss is 10% of the input, being evaporation with no realisable value. The actual output is 2,200 kg. The cost per kg of the output is:
The sale proceeds of scrap arising out of the materials used on a particular job are treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: Income of the business credited to the financial Profit and Loss Account only
options.B: A reduction of the factory overheads of the whole factory
options.C: A general income to be shared by all jobs of the period
options.D: A credit to that particular job, reducing the cost of the job

q: A machine costs Rs 9,00,000 and is expected to have a scrap value of Rs 1,00,000 after producing a total output of 2,00,000 units. Depreciation is charged by the production units method. The output during the year is 25,000 units. The depreciation charge for the year is:
The main practical disadvantage of using separate departmental (multiple) overhead absorption rates, as against a single rate, is that departmental rates:

options.A: Cannot be used where service departments exist in the factory
options.B: Always result in under-absorption of overheads
options.C: Are prohibited where job costing is followed
options.D: Involve considerably more clerical work, records and cost in their computation and application

q: The total cost of power for a factory is Rs 2,60,000. Department A has machines of 50 HP which run for 2,000 hours and Department B has machines of 30 HP which run for 1,000 hours. The power cost is apportioned on the basis of HP-hours worked. The share of the power cost borne by Department A is:
The cost of training newly recruited workers, during the period of their training, is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: Direct labour cost of the jobs on which the trainees happen to work
options.B: A loss charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.C: A deduction from the wages payable to the trainees
options.D: Factory (works) overheads of the period

q: A power station incurs total costs of Rs 21,60,000 and generates 12,00,000 units of electricity. In transmission and distribution, 10% of the units generated are lost. The cost per unit of electricity sold is:
In railway traffic costing, the cost of empty running — wagons and coaches hauled empty to the points where traffic offers — is treated as:

options.A: A part of the cost of the loaded (revenue-earning) movement, which must bear it
options.B: A loss of the Railways written off without allocation to any traffic
options.C: A cost recovered separately from the consignors of the return loads only
options.D: A capital cost to be charged to the cost of new lines

q: Three workers in a gang work 40 hours each during a week at time rates of Rs 60, Rs 50 and Rs 40 per hour respectively. The gang earns total piece wages of Rs 9,000 for the week, which are distributed among the workers in proportion to their time wages. The share of the worker with the highest time rate is:

Where under-absorbed or over-absorbed overheads at the end of a period arise from seasonal or cyclical fluctuations which are expected to reverse and cancel out within the same accounting year, the difference is generally:

options.A: Written off immediately to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.B: Adjusted at once through a supplementary rate to all jobs of the period
options.C: Ignored altogether and never recorded in the cost accounts
options.D: Carried forward as a deferred balance to be adjusted in the remaining part of the year

q: Material issued to a job is 500 kg purchased at Rs 20 per kg. Normal wastage in using the material is 2% of the quantity issued, and the wastage is sold at Rs 5 per kg. The net material cost charged to the job is:
The work-in-progress (job) ledger maintained under the cost ledger system contains:

options.A: An individual account for each job or process in progress, and its total balance agrees with the work-in-progress control account
options.B: Accounts of all the debtors to whom finished goods have been sold
options.C: The personal accounts of the workers showing wages due to them
options.D: A record only of the materials lying in the stores awaiting issue

q: A transport undertaking has a fleet of 20 vehicles. The total operating cost for a month of 25 working days is Rs 6,00,000. The operating cost per vehicle-day is:
Expenditure incurred on the development of a specific new product, from which benefit is expected over the production life of that product, is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: A general overhead of the year in which it is incurred, like ordinary research cost
options.B: A financial expense excluded from the cost accounts altogether
options.C: Direct material cost of the first batch of the product produced
options.D: Deferred revenue expenditure, carried forward and written off against the production of that product
